What to Watch for in the 2026 U.S. Midterms

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-27 15:19 UTC

With the first U.S. midterm elections since President Donald Trump’s return to the White House approaching, voters will be weighing in on a range of issues, from the economy and rising cost of living, to the administration’s foreign policy and the future direction of both major parties. At a recent virtual Nieman-to-Nieman seminar, a group of Nieman alums who cover politics discussed what they’re hearing from voters with regards to key Senate races, the growing influence of younger voters drawn to progressive candidates, and the political implications of conflicts involving Iran, Ukraine, and Russia. Moderated by Austin Bogues (NF ’21), news desk editor at USA Today, the discussion brought together James Barragán (NF ’24), political anchor for Spectrum News in Austin, Texas; Bill Barrow (NF ’22), national politics reporter for The Associated Press in Atlanta; and Ines Pohl (NF ’05), Washington bureau chief and White House correspondent for Deutsche Welle, Germany’s international public broadcaster.

India Targets Journalists in Crackdown on Growing Protest Movement

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-19 21:20 UTC

As protests continue across India over allegations of government corruption, dozens of members of the media have been subjected to arrest, detainment and assault, according to witnesses, press rights organizations, and the journalists themselves. Thousands of protesters have taken to the streets of New Delhi in recent weeks, demanding the resignation of election officials allegedly tied to the deletion of nearly 130 million names from voter registration rolls. The protests — which have largely been organized by the Cockroach Janata Party, so named after India's chief justice called the nation’s unemployed youth and activists "cockroaches" — are part of a wider wave of youth discontent aimed at Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his administration. Organizers have mobilized young people via social media, tapping into frustrations with government corruption, eroding trust in democratic institutions, and a lack of access to jobs and educational opportunities.

Testing the Legal Limits of Press Access

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-15 14:51 UTC

The Trump administration’s latest attacks on the news media have followed a familiar pattern: President Donald Trump lashes out at news outlets for perceived bias and follows up with restrictive actions that appear blatantly unconstitutional; a judge’s ruling follows, temporarily halting the actions; and the administration pivots and pushes ahead with other restrictions. This time it was the removal of three outlets — CNN, MS NOW, and Politico — from White House press access in September. After the groups sued, and U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly issued a temporary restraining order restoring their access on Sept. 24, the administration barred CNN and Politico from providing pool coverage on trips outside Washington. Kelly issued a longer, preliminary injunction on Oct. 14, halting the administration from blocking the news organizations’ access to the White House while the case proceeds. This Newsroom Wants You to Be Part of the Journey Before It Even Starts

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-06 10:00 UTC

My happiest times in journalism have been when I have built something new. For my latest venture, I want to help bring investigative journalism on climate and environmental issues to a much larger audience than it has reached in the past. To do so, I’m starting a brand-new newsroom focused on the environmental and climate crisis, and I’m taking my audience along for the ride. I’ll be documenting every facet of the process with an “open kitchen” approach of radical transparency, starting with a 100-day video countdown chronicling all the steps involved with starting a news organization from the ground up. This effort combines two of the things I’m most passionate about: I love digging up stories that other people don’t want to see published, and I love creating opportunities for other journalists. I’ve been a journalist for most of my life. I started working at age 14 for the local paper in my rural German town, turned to doing investigative stories in my early 20s, and later studied investigative journalism at the Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism in New York.

America’s Shrinking Local Newsrooms, Through a Photographer’s Lens

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-02 12:30 UTC

For many journalists, the sight of empty desks is a sadly familiar one. My first glimpse of a gutted newsroom facing further cutbacks sparked a documentary photography project that has so far taken me to more than 50 newsrooms across the United States over the past eight years. It began when my mother, a loyal subscriber to our local metro in southern Illinois, told me a decade ago how disappointed she was in the newspaper. She complained that the local coverage was lacking, and the paper seemed to be thinner. Already several years into my photojournalism career, I was unsurprised by her remarks — I had been witnessing the decline of print media since graduation from journalism school. Still, my curiosity was piqued, and I arranged a visit to the paper to see for myself. Cue the scene of a barren newsroom. Not only were there empty desks, but also an expanse of exposed carpet with indentations showing where desks had once long stood. While there has been a great deal of reporting on the issues plaguing local journalism, I hadn’t seen the story told visually.

Seven Takeaways on Convenience and News

Nieman Reports · 2026-09-25 14:53 UTC

"Against Convenience: Embracing Friction in an Age of Endless Ease" was released on Sept.15, 2026, by Hanover Square Press, an imprint of HarperCollins Publishers. Courtesy of Hanover Square Press From the earliest pitch, I knew that I wanted to cover the news industry in my book, “Against Convenience.” The book looks at the technology around us and asks whether it’s really improving our lives. Is delivery food worth the higher price? Is streaming music better than collecting CDs or MP3s? News embodies the paradox of modern convenience: We have access to more information than ever before, but misinformation and partisanship are rampant and the purveyors of reliable information are struggling to stay solvent. Plus, I figured if I was going to criticize other fields — tech, entertainment, appliance manufacturing — I couldn’t avoid my own. I don’t know how interested the average nonjournalist is in the day-to-day operations of the news business, so I tried to look in the mirror more than gaze at my navel.

澳枪击事件嫌疑人为父子：曾宣誓效忠“伊斯兰国”，行凶枪支为合法持有

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-16 02:23 UTC

据新华社12月15日援引澳大利亚广播公司报道，澳大利亚联合反恐小组调查人员表示，悉尼邦迪滩枪击事件两名嫌疑人曾宣誓效忠“伊斯兰国”恐怖组织。 报道援引联合反恐小组一名不愿透露姓名的高级官员的话说，警方在邦迪滩两名枪手车内发现一面“伊斯兰国”旗帜。澳大利亚安全情报组织6年前就已在调查邦迪滩枪击案两名枪手之一的纳维德·阿克拉姆，他与“伊斯兰国”在悉尼的恐怖分子有密切联系。 澳大利亚警方表示，枪击事件的两名嫌疑人是父子关系，使用合法获得的枪支发动了此次袭击事件。 澳大利亚总理阿尔巴尼斯15日表示：“今天下午4点， 我将把更严格的枪支法律列入国家内阁的议程，包括限制个人可持有或许可的枪支数量 。此外，还需对许可证进行定期审查。人们的情况会发生变化，人们的思想也会随着时间的推移而变得激进。许可证不应永久有效。” 此次枪击事件已造成包括1名作案嫌疑人在内的16人死亡、40人受伤。这是自1996年塔斯马尼亚州亚瑟港枪击事件造成35人死亡以来，澳大利亚发生的最严重的大规模枪击事件。 持有枪支许可证长达十年 据多家外媒报道，其中一名袭击者为24岁的澳大利亚公民纳维德·阿克拉姆，他在现场被捕，随后被送往悉尼的一家医院。另一名袭击者是他的父亲萨吉德·阿克拉姆，他于1998年来到澳大利亚，被警方当场击毙。 澳大利亚警方随后证实，纳维德·阿克拉姆此前已被新南威尔士州警方和其他机构记录在案。其父亲萨吉德·阿克拉姆持有枪支许可证，名下登记有6支枪，目前均已被追回。新南威尔士州警察局长马尔·兰永透露，萨吉德·阿克拉姆已持有枪支许可证长达十年。 阿尔巴尼斯在新闻发布会上透露，纳维德·阿克拉姆曾于2019年10月首次引起当局的注意。他补充说，对该男子进行检查是基于他与其他人有联系，但评估结果表明，没有任何迹象表明他存在持续的威胁或暴力倾向。 新南威尔士州州长克里斯·明斯表示，警方正在调查他们的系统是否存在故障，导致合法持有的武器可能被用于恐怖袭击。 枪手“性格古怪”，爱好打猎 据《卫报》澳大利亚版报道，纳维德·阿克拉姆在袭击前从事砌砖工作。他的同事表示，纳维德性格古怪，“没人和他亲近”。“（砌砖工人）在一起的时间很长，因为砌砖是一项非常枯燥乏味的工作，所以大家会聊很多话。但纳维德是一个性格很古怪的人……他工作非常努力，几乎没有休息日。” 尽管澳大利亚警方并未确认纳维德·阿克拉姆是否合法持有枪支，但据这位同事表示，纳维德经常外出打猎，曾提及在昆士兰州南部高原的克鲁克韦尔附近射杀兔子和其他猎物。这位同事还表示，就在几周前，纳维德告诉老板，他的手骨折了，所以要到2026年才能工作。

在校园里，孩子们时常举起戴在手腕上的手表，彼此一碰，便加为好友。 这种以“安全”为核心卖点的儿童电话手表，如今已超越通信工具的属性，悄然演变成一个拥有独特规则、社交层级甚至灰色产业链的未成年人数字社交圈——“小天才圈”。 在这个属于他们的“江湖”里，“大佬榜”备受关注，“扩列”（增加好友）成为新的社交需求，“点主”（在主页点赞）是每日必做的功课……这些让成年人感到陌生的词汇，正构筑着未成年人的数字社交世界。 然而，伴随着这种社交形态的兴起，家长们的担忧也日益加剧：孩子过度沉迷手表社交、不良信息传播、因品牌壁垒导致的“社交绑架”等问题逐渐浮现。《法治日报》记者近日对该现象展开调查，试图揭开这一未成年人数字社交圈的真实面貌。 点赞成社交“硬通货” 据北京“小天才圈”资深玩家陈曦（化名）介绍，圈内有5000余名活跃用户，多为11岁至17岁的学生，这个社交圈形成了一套精心设计的“混圈规则”。“入圈”需设定两个字的独特圈名，随后可在平台分享生活点滴，吸引具有相同爱好的好友进行互动；若想提升知名度或影响力，需每日经营主页并与好友动态互动。 记者注意到，在一些社交平台上，大量以“小天才圈交友攻略”为主题的内容应运而生，内容涵盖如何快速“扩列”、获取更多点赞等“实用”技巧，评论区有不少“留下ID互加好友”的留言。在这一社交体系中，点赞是这套规则的核心——平台设定每日主页获赞上限为3000个，若要达到“100万+”的“大佬”级别，需连续点赞近一年时间。围绕点赞数与知名度，圈内形成了清晰的“大佬排行榜”，点赞数也成为社交“硬通货”。 这种对点赞的追逐，已催生出相关服务产业。记者调查发现，某社交平台上，拥有数十万甚至上百万点赞数的账号，售价从几百元到上千元不等：100多万点赞的账号标价1300元，90多万点赞的账号标价1200元。 今年18岁的“灵师”（圈名），在2021年14岁时加入“小天才圈”，她的账号目前已拥有150个好友、超100万点赞量。她告诉记者，这样的账号市场价值约1000元。 “围绕点赞需求，还衍生出代刷赞、租账号、出售‘大佬好友位’等服务。”“灵师”进一步介绍，例如付费100元至180元，即可获得“bot”（记者注：“bot”是一种第三方开发的自动化工具，主要用于刷赞、修改记录和发送动态等功能，这类工具能帮助用户快速提升账号点赞数，从而在未成年人社交圈中获得更高地位）自动点赞功能——用户将手表寄给相关人员进行10天左右的处理便能完成安装。此后，发帖5分钟内即可自动获赞，还可以一键查询未点赞名单。

产地造假、年份速成、无视监管！央视曝光新会陈皮市场乱象

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-15 08:23 UTC

近日，总台接到群众举报，反映陈皮市场存在年份虚标、产地及工艺造假等问题，千元一斤的“年份陈皮”亦可能名不副实。 茶枝柑新果皮冒充陈皮 广西浦北出现“速成工艺陈皮” 记者发现，直播间里售卖陈皮低价轮番轰炸，年份承诺掷地有声。 直播间也有主播爆料，八成市面上所谓广东新会陈皮实为广西陈皮。 广西钦州市浦北县是茶枝柑重要种植基地，其果皮是陈皮风味“越陈越香”关键，也是浦北陈皮唯一原料。2024年当地陈皮产业产值破60亿元，采收季大量鲜果加工晾晒成柑皮。 果农和收购商称，今年浦北茶枝柑鲜果收购价走低。按20斤鲜果出1斤柑皮比例，叠加人工成本，品相好的新柑皮成本约30元/斤，低端柑皮仅六七元，且当年新柑皮并非真正陈皮。 这家企业的负责人告诉记者，按行业共识与团体标准，柑皮需陈化三年以上才可称为陈皮，陈化时间越长价值越高，但他透露，自然陈化需长期积压资金，多数企业是难以承受的。 这家企业的负责人私下告诉记者，为缓解资金占用压力，一种名为“轻工艺”的速成加工方式，眼下正在部分陈皮生产企业里流行，他们仅需一个月的时间，就能将新采收的茶枝柑果皮处理为外观近似三年、五年自然陈化过的陈皮，这样做能大幅缩短陈化周期、降低企业的运营成本。 浦北自然陈化五年陈皮批发价每斤150元至200元，企业造假“工艺皮”成本仅70元左右，高额利润促使更多商家放弃自然陈化、铤而走险。 记者离开企业，在广西浦北县柑浦堂健康产业有限公司分拣车间，再次见到大批量造假“工艺皮”陈皮，同一批“工艺皮”因加工受热差异形成色差，被分拣标注为三年、五年等不同年份。 负责人透露，不同年份“工艺皮”本质相同，批发价均70元左右一斤，零售价差极大，标五年款卖500元一斤，标十年款卖1000元一斤，仅凭外观就能翻倍抬价，利润超成本十倍以上。 新会陈皮从浦北进货 “工艺皮”贴上陈皮标签以假乱真 浦北与新会陈皮原料同为茶枝柑，仅产地不同，新会较高生产成本使当地部分头部商家常年从浦北拿货，浦北成其重要原料供应地。 记者在柑浦堂分拣仓库看到，大量标注“新会陈皮”“新会特产”的纸箱正打包“工艺皮”，这些广西陈皮每日批量发往广东新会，造假供需链路已成熟稳定。 记者发现，浦北当地部分规模企业和小型收购商，已形成了这种“工艺皮”的造假供应体系，可自主加工或快速调配各类“年份”陈皮货品，个别企业年销新会原料数量惊人。 随后经浦北陈皮企业负责人引荐，记者见到多位专程从新会赴浦北采购的商家，他们坦言同时经营新会皮与浦北皮，外地“工艺皮”因价格低廉成电商供货重要选择。

《怦然心动》导演莱纳与妻子在家中遇害，警方尚未证实是其子所杀

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-15 07:23 UTC

当地时间12月14日，曾执导《怦然心动》《当哈利遇到莎莉》《危情十日》等影片的美国导演罗伯·莱纳（Rob Reiner）在他位于洛杉矶的家中遇害身亡。洛杉矶警察已对外证实，现年78岁的莱纳与他现年68岁的妻子米歇尔·辛格·莱纳（Michele Singer Reiner）的遗体一同被发现。 2019年，罗伯·莱纳（左一）与《当哈利遇到莎莉》的主演梅格·瑞恩、比利·克里斯托出席TMC经典电影节。 据悉，洛杉矶消防局的人员于当地时间12月14日下午3点38分接到医疗救助电话，赶赴位于布伦特伍德区的一处住宅中，随后发现两人已死亡。当天晚间，洛杉矶警察局在其社交媒体官方账号确认死者为导演罗伯·莱纳夫妇，将由抢劫凶杀部门主导调查。而好莱坞媒体TMZ援引执法部门消息称，“两人身上有与刀具造成的伤口相符的割裂伤。” 好莱坞媒体《每日野兽》称，有消息人士向他们透露，是两人的女儿罗米最先发现他们倒在血泊中；罗伯·莱纳当时已死亡，妻子米歇尔在救护车送院途中离世。 此外，《人物》杂志称通过多方消息，得知莱纳夫妇系被他们的儿子尼克（Nick）所杀害。不过，这一说法并未获得警方的证实。罗伯·莱纳与摄影师米歇尔·辛格相识于《当哈利遇到莎莉》拍摄时期，两人于1989 年结婚，育有三个子女，分别为杰克（Jake）、尼克（Nick）和罗米（Romy）。 2014年，罗伯·莱纳与妻子偕三名子女杰克、罗米、尼克（右三至右一）出席活动。 《人物》杂志还在报道中指出：尼克2016年接受其采访时，曾谈到自己长达数年的毒品成瘾经历。这段经历始于他十几岁出头，导致他一度流落街头。他表示，大约从15岁开始，便反复进出戒毒康复机构；随着成瘾问题不断加重，他逐渐与家人疏远，并在多个州经历了长时间的无家可归生活。 2025年9月15日，罗伯·莱纳在纽约出席活动。视觉中国 图 获取更多RSS： https://feedx.net https://feedx.site

演员何晴追悼会举行，其子追思母亲：北京这场雪像是为她而下

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-15 06:53 UTC

一场雪落，人间倩影化雪归天。 12月15日上午，众多剧迷粉丝冒着严寒赶到北京昌平殡仪馆久安厅，送别演员何晴最后一程。12月13日，这位被誉为“古典第一美人”的演员因病去世，终年61岁。 不到10点，殡仪馆告别厅外已经站满了前来悼念的观众和粉丝，有人胸前佩戴小白花，有人手捧鲜花，一位浙江的网友还托人送来了悼念花圈。 “何晴的作品在我们心中留下了太多美好回忆，她的演技和性格都让我们深深喜爱，这次听到她突然去世的消息，我们非常意外，来到这里也是一种悼念。”一位何晴的影迷说。 现场粉丝在悼念簿上写下对何晴的话，不到一会儿，悼念簿就已写满对她的怀念。一位观众用清秀的字迹写下：“亲爱的何晴，我们的童年、青春都在您的影视作品中得到陪伴。美丽可人的何晴，很痛心听到您的消息，我代表我的同学们来这为你送行。” 曾在电视剧《水浒传》中饰演卢俊义的演员王卫国也来到现场，神色哀切。他说自己和何晴既是邻居，也是多年好友，在他印象中何晴是一个温婉、暖心的人，没有架子，总是远远地和人打招，笑嘻嘻地说话。何晴生病时常给王卫国打电话，请他送自己去医院。即便病重时，何晴也保持乐观积极的态度，王卫国有些事情想不开，她还来开导自己。“何晴走了，我们都很难过。只要你记住她，她就永远还在。”王卫国说。 《水浒传》中卢俊义的扮演者王卫国 《西游记》中万圣公主扮演者张青深情回忆何晴往事：“我们是小时候就认识的好朋友，从80年代到现在，有缘分做了这些年的朋友。她说话慢慢的，很甜很温柔。” 《西游记》中万圣公主扮演者张青 在广大观众的真挚请求下，原本仅面向亲友的告别仪式临时对外开放，大家排着队，秩序井然地进入灵堂，与这位“荧屏中的温婉佳人、生活中的坚韧女性”做最后的道别。 久安厅内的屏幕上滚动播放着何晴的照片，厅内四周摆满了亲友的花圈，其中包括六小龄童、唐国强、翁虹、尤勇智等何晴圈内好友送来的花圈，还有《三国演义》剧组送来的花圈。人群中不时传来一阵抽泣。 何晴之子许何代表亲友致悼词。他回忆了何晴对抗病魔的乐观积极，以及作为母亲对孩子深深的爱和眷恋。 许何说，妈妈很喜欢下雪，经常在雪后穿一件毛茸茸的衣服外出赏雪。“今年12月12日北京下了第一场雪，我摸着妈妈的脸跟她说北京下雪了，下得好大，好像很久都没有下过这么大的雪。在我的心里，这场雪好像是刻意为她下的。12月13日早晨天空晴朗，白色的雪布满了大地，我妈妈在她最喜欢的早晨离开了大家，去了天国，远离了所有的疾病和痛苦。” 何晴，1964年1月13日出生于浙江衢州江山市。她是中国内地唯一一位演遍四大名著影视作品的女演员，被誉为“古典第一美女”。

Little gain for American patients, real harm for European ones: Why Europe must answer the US' most-favoured-nation pricing as a Union

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-11-10 00:00 UTC

The US administration ties the prices it pays for medicines to those paid abroad and justifies this ‘most-favoured-nation’ policy with the claim that Americans subsidise low prices in Europe. This column describes how the available evidence shows that most-favoured nation risks imposing substantial costs on European health systems for a modest American gain. Moreover, its justification cannot be sustained: lower European prices do not cause higher American ones, and American prices are no benchmark for a fair contribution to innovation. Europe should respond as a Union, close its gap in capital and scale, and coordinate targeted incentives at EU level.

Making work pay for married mothers: Two simple fixes to US tax credits

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-11-10 00:00 UTC

Only about two-thirds of US mothers with young children are in the labour force. For many low-income married mothers, taking a job barely pays: most face participation tax rates above 25%, rising to 60% once childcare costs are counted. This column argues that lifting the caps on the childcare credit and basing the Earned Income Tax Credit on the primary earner’s income alone would each raise maternal employment. Together, they could raise it by almost 13 points, from 59% to 72%. Both reforms largely pay for themselves.

Energy labels, feebates and standards: Lessons from the EU’s 2021 reform

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-11-09 00:00 UTC

The European Commission is simplifying the rules around the EU energy label. This column uses product-level sales data on refrigerators in Belgium, France, Germany, and Poland to evaluate the impact on energy use of the 2021 switch from the inflated A+++/A++/A+ scale to a more informative A–G scale. Although consumers prefer better-rated products, they value one euro of future electricity costs at only 42–79 cents. Relabeling alone reduces average electricity use per refrigerator sold by 0.7–2.2%, but other policies would be more effective: a revenue-neutral feebate would reduce electricity use by 2–6% and a stricter minimum standard by 10–16%, at the cost of higher prices.

Similarity is not exposure: Measuring spillovers from US–China trade frictions

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-11-09 00:00 UTC

The redirection of Chinese exports away from the US has fuelled concerns about its spillovers to other countries. This column shows why trade-basket similarity can be a misleading measure of exposure and introduces four simple, theory-consistent indices: export competition, import competition, consumer gains, and sourcing gains. They produce different country rankings and reveal how competitive losses can coexist with gains from cheaper goods and inputs. Thus, the response to spillovers from the surge in Chinese exports should be guided by where the shock actually lands, not by which countries look most like China.

When wording changes what we find: The impact of inflation expectations on spending

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-11-08 00:00 UTC

How households’ inflation expectations affect their spending is a central question for researchers and policymakers alike. Yet empirical evidence remains mixed. This column shows that the consumption question researchers choose can change the sign and strength of the estimated relationship. Questions about spending attitudes and plans yield negative associations with expected inflation, while questions about past spending yield weakly positive or insignificant associations. Differences in question type matter much more than reference unit or recall horizon. Treating these measures as interchangeable can lead to misleading conclusions about the expectations channel of monetary policy.

Target What? The Foundations of Poverty Targeting -- by Rema Hanna, Emily Breza, Benjamin A. Olken, Abhijit Banerjee, Arun G. Chandrasekhar, Gideon Moore

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Most government transfer programs aim to target the poor. Doing so implicitly assumes that the lowest-consumption households have the highest marginal social valuation, i.e., have the highest social welfare gain from an additional dollar. But this need not be the case. In 600 Indonesian villages, we ask over 5,500 villagers to rank other villagers on how well off they are and how much a modest cash transfer would help them, and compare these rankings to consumption and self-assessed welfare. Targeting consumption misses 77% of households with the highest marginal social valuation. Targeting self-assessed welfare misses 57%. Even targeting those the community ranks worst off in levels, not margins, misses 25%. Divergences between different notions of neediness are statistically predictable. In a randomized controlled trial, proxy means tests best target consumption, self-targeting ordeals capture self-assessed welfare levels, and community targeting comes closest to marginal social valuation. Targeting strategies inescapably embed normative stances.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Unconventional Monetary Policy and Deposit Retention -- by Philip Strahan, Tuo Yang

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

The two dimensions of unconventional monetary policy — holding the short rate at the zero-lower bound (ZLB) and quantitative easing (QE) — shifted deposit composition toward more interest-sensitive customers. The ZLB drew these customers by creating rate compression, which limited the benefit of searching for high-yielding liquidity sources. QE also drew rate-sensitive, large depositors from the Federal Reserve’s purchases of bonds from non-banks. Once policy normalized, flow sensitivity and the deposit beta both increased with exposure to QE and the ZLB. We conclude that unconventional monetary policy made deposit retention costlier and riskier for banks.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Debiasing Law Enforcement Officers: Evidence from an Expressive Arts Intervention in India -- by Sofia Amaral, Girija Borker, Nishith Prakash, María Micaela Sviatschi

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Frontline state agents exercise substantial discretion over citizens’ access to public services, yet little is known about whether the attitudes and beliefs shaping this discretion can be changed among incumbent bureaucrats. Partnering with the Bihar Police - one of India’s largest states that operates under comparatively severe policing capacity constraints, we conduct a cluster randomized controlled trial across 417 police stations and roughly 2,500 active duty senior field police officers to evaluate a three-day expressive arts intervention, grounded in the Theatre of the Oppressed, designed to change police responses to gender-based violence (GBV). Approximately 7 months after baseline, treated officers exhibit more favorable attitudes toward GBV, greater empathy, and stronger legal knowledge.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

TaskNet: Building Occupational Task Inventories from Worker Interviews at Scale -- by Jennifer Wang, Andreas Haupt, Isaac Robinson, Phil Lewis, Erik Brynjolfsson, Diyi Yang

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Understanding how AI is reshaping work requires an accurate account of the tasks workers perform. Workers are often the first to see how their jobs are changing, as new responsibilities and tools often appear in everyday work before these changes reach formal descriptions. Interviews with workers can help capture these emerging changes in job tasks. Yet existing methods support standardized ratings across workers, while open-ended conversations with workers remain costly to collect and synthesize at scale. We introduce the Stanford Task Network (TaskNet), an occupational taxonomy grounded directly in workers’ accounts of their everyday work. To construct TaskNet, we develop a mixed-initiative system that induces task inventories directly from workers. The system conducts interviews, standardizes reports into individual task lists, and aggregates these lists into occupational task inventories.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

The Hidden Sharpe Ratio -- by Mikhail Chernov, Bryan T. Kelly, Semyon Malamud, Johannes Schwab

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

We estimate the maximal Sharpe ratio in large cross-sections of assets directly, without constructing the efficient portfolio. Covariance estimation in this setting requires regularization, which suppresses the contribution of small-eigenvalue directions. Our estimator progressively recovers this contribution, yielding tight upper and lower bounds with asymptotic confidence intervals. We further show that ridge-regularized Markowitz portfolios, the construction underlying many existing high-Sharpe benchmarks, deliver out-of-sample Sharpe ratios that fall short of the true maximum by an explicit, non-vanishing multiplicative factor. Applied to U.S. equities, the method delivers an estimated maximal annualized Sharpe ratio of approximately 7.4, or 5.0 once micro-cap stocks are excluded, substantially exceeding existing portfolio-based benchmarks of 1.0–4.0. Adding corporate bonds raises the maximum, though not by a statistically significant margin. Nonlinear portfolio weights dominate linear ones, and characteristics introduced after 2004 contribute little additional Sharpe ratio.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Clearing the Fog: Price Transparency, Market Churn, and Consumer Welfare in Short-Term Rentals -- by Ginger Zhe Jin, Liad Wagman, Jingyi Xing

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

We study California's short-term lodging price transparency law (AB 537), which from July 1, 2024 required Airbnb and other providers to advertise fee-inclusive prices. Using Coarsened Exact Matching to compare Airbnb listings in San Diego and San Francisco with those in Seattle and Chicago, we find that all-in pricing made guests more price-sensitive relative to control cities; yet, contrary to the standard prediction that transparency lowers prices, average daily rates rose by 4.8 percent. We also observe significant market churn: relative to control cities, treated cities saw more exits and entries, listings reliant on cleaning-fee revenue disproportionately exited, higher-quality listings were more likely to stay, and entrants offered lower fees and lower quality than incumbents. A discrete-choice welfare analysis shows that the law removed a sizable “welfare illusion” created by obscured fees and, largely through market churn, raised realized consumer surplus.

Lightcone Commons: what I funded and why

LessWrong · 2026-11-10 05:13 UTC

I am an evaluator for Lightcone Commons (LC). LC is a platform for applicants to submit projects, for evaluators to rank them and for funders to choose the funding orders of several evaluators. It is not a foundation, in that it doesn’t have money that it spends how it chooses. And I do not have a permanent position working for Lightcone Commons. I get paid 2% of any money that a funder chooses to direct via my funding order. This pays for my time and also for any research that I pay others to do. That said, what were my general and specific funding preferences? This is a version of what Lightcone published, it might be wrong, but theirs was definitely wrong (their headline numbers didn’t include funding that had been hidden) Lightcone also has a beautiful page for looking through public information here. General preferences: I like AI policy that creates the ability to slow down AI if necessary, but doesn’t automatically push for immediate pauses. I like policy orgs which people I know in US politics respect.

Live disagreements with people around me

LessWrong · 2026-11-10 05:01 UTC

I’m pretty interested in conveying the costs of letting AI development proceed unchecked to the general public. In relation to this, I feel like I run into a lot of disagreements with people around me. Misc very quickly written points on which my own impression has seemed very different from others in recent months: 1. It’s way, way, way more important that we stop dangerous AI soon than that we ensure that we don’t stop AI too much I have the sense the sophisticated and worldly position here is to be very concerned about ‘over-regulation’ and about not doing exactly the right regulations. But it’s an obvious pragmatic fact that the stakes of overregulation are minuscule compared to the stakes of underregulating here. And the stakes of mis-regulation are very often going to be unintended slowing, which is in the same bucket. 2. If we stopped AI development, the risk of not starting up again for an extremely long time is low This one just feels kind of crazy to me, like I may be missing something.

OpenAtom and Elemental

LessWrong · 2026-11-10 04:52 UTC

2012 Compact nuclear power had long been considered intractable for civilian use. But on a cold December day, at an alternative energy conference, a team of academics reveals a new discovery: charging up small nuclear reactors over several days at high energy can produce clean power output. It is not yet competitive with other energy sources, but it does seem promising. The name of this new technology is Compact Nuclear Power (CNP). Some note that at larger energy loads, CNP cores might become unstable, leading to meltdowns or explosions. The risks remain theoretical for now. OpenAtom Fuel materials and CNP core design continue to improve. ExxonMobil releases some early commercially viable cores. It is becoming clear that this technology will be transformative—at minimum, it will accelerate world energy production at a time that it is greatly needed, and some even say that it will unlock transmutation, creating plentiful quantities of various elements from feedstock.

Eyesight as a replicator, with genes as its vehicle

LessWrong · 2026-11-10 04:47 UTC

Dear reader, this post will be completed in some hours; I'm posting it now because I'm participating in justwrite.club and I don't want to forfeit $1k. I'll remove this note when it's done. That said, the sections that are below are real; what I'm still doing is adding the "coming soon" sections. ---- Or: The payload lens on Darwin Tl;dr: What is the most natural teleological shorthand to use, when thinking about evolution? The “gene-centered view” of e.g. Dawkins says: genes are “trying” to increase the number of exact copies of themselves. And organisms are “vehicles” genes use to survive. The “payload lens” (which I’ll be pitching) says: adaptive payloads (such as eyesight or fair meiosis) are “trying” to become deeper, stabler attractor basins that can team up with other adaptive payloads. And genes are “vehicles” these payloads use to survive.

Pulling the Lever in a Subway Problem

LessWrong · 2026-11-10 03:40 UTC

Eleven years ago I was on the Red Line (not the section that's a trolley), and found myself in a variant of the classic moral dilemma. I wrote about it on Reddit at the time: Hi! I'm the person who pulled the brake. What I saw: The train starts pulling out of the station. Someone begins shouting that their arm is caught in the door. I look over, see that the door is closed somewhere between their elbow and wrist, but it's not clear exactly where with their jacket on. People, including me, start shouting to pull the brake, but no one does. The train keeps accelerating, and it looks to me like once we get to the end of the station they're going to lose their hand. I get to the back of the car and pull the brake. After the train stops, the man manages to pull his arm into the train, with his bag still on the outside. If he'd let go of his bag I think he would have been able to do this sooner, but he was panicking as I suspect most people would with their arm half out of the train like that.

Lightcone Commons: Round 1 complete, Round 2 underway

LessWrong · 2026-11-10 01:43 UTC

Tl;dr: Lightcone Commons’ first funding round is complete! 17 evaluators made funding recommendations, including Zvi Mowshowitz, Scott Siskind and Eliezer Yudkowsky. 23 funders coordinated to grant $45.1M, and 147 projects received funding. Round two is open. Applications for round two close on November 15th and funders confirm their grants by December 14th. Funders can join anytime before December 7th. In 2027, we will be hosting funding rounds monthly. Yes. Every month. You can join as a funder, express interest in joining as an evaluator, and apply for funding at lightconecommons.com. Lightcone Commons staff do not decide what grants get made.[1] Pls stop saying that "Lightcone Commons funded us", that's a bit like saying "PayPal funded me". Lightcone Commons is an end-to-end philanthropic coordination platform. We host an open funding application, and invite evaluators to make ordered funding recommendations. Participating funders then decide how much they want to give, and to whom – either by following the recommendations of evaluators or choosing specific projects to fund.

George Lucas spent 17 years building his latest world. This one you can walk through.

Big Think · 2026-11-09 16:27 UTC

What happens to us after we die is a fundamental question of human civilization, and anxieties about succession lurk beneath every human story: Will my work live on? Will my children pass on good values? Have I done my duty? Our rituals, religions, sacred sites, and art all seek to answer these big questions, yet none can conclusively, or we wouldn’t keep asking. I could feel these existential questions in the air as I walked past huge models of Star Wars spaceships alongside a Frida Kahlo self-portrait in the galleries of Los Angeles’ new Lucas Museum of Narrative Art — a tribute to human storytelling through visual art that filmmaker George Lucas and his wife, Mellody Hobson, a Chicago-born investor and civic leader, worked on for nearly 17 years. After a lifetime of creating and collecting exceptionally popular narrative art, what happens to these ideas and objects when their 82-year-old creator and cataloguer, George Lucas, is gone? And what happens to his reputation, his legacy — himself?

Are you really who you think you are?

Big Think · 2026-11-09 14:00 UTC

Who are you? You might think you know, but science offers a more complicated answer. In fact, Lisa Feldman Barrett, PhD, a University Distinguished Professor of Psychology at Northeastern University, says the inquiry may be unanswerable. A question that can be answered: Who are you in a given moment? Take, for example, someone who has a habit of interrupting while others are talking. They may see themselves as engaged — so enthusiastic that they’re compelled to interject with what they think the speaker is about to say. The person being interrupted, meanwhile, may experience their conversation partner as rude. So, do the interrupter’s intentions matter more than how they’re perceived? According to Barrett, no. The perception of rudeness is just as real — not because it matters more than the interrupter’s intentions, but because it matters just as much. “The characteristics or traits that we think are inherent to a person are not inherent to that person,” she says. “They exist to describe that person in relation to other conditions.

Five systems L&D can build to protect focus at work

Big Think · 2026-11-09 12:53 UTC

Many organizational cultures are out of balance. Senior leaders face an emerging tension that often goes unnoticed unless they are looking. In fact, it’s the very technology created to accelerate productivity and performance is quietly eroding both, and potentially, much more. Digital connectivity – from smartphones to social media, AI to applications – that has enabled faster decisions, global collaboration, and real-time responsiveness – has become a double-edged sword. For the myriad gains technology has delivered, we’re also paying a cognitive tax. In fact, the attention crisis, a burnout epidemic, and a degradation in decision quality are reshaping the global workforce in consequential ways. Leaders today face a paradox: leveraging technology to increase effectiveness while also protecting the health and well-being of the very people whose effectiveness they depend upon. This balance can no longer be treated as a matter of personal productivity. Digital distraction has become an organizational risk.

In a big star-forming nebula, JWST finds the smallest failed stars

Big Think · 2026-11-09 07:00 UTC

In astronomy, the brightest objects dominate the light we receive. This image shows the central region of the Tarantula Nebula in the Large Magellanic Cloud. The young and dense star cluster R136 can be seen near the center of the image. The tidal forces exerted on the Large Magellanic Cloud by the Milky Way are triggering a wave of star-formation in there, which happens to be the largest star-forming region known in the Local Group. R136a1, at the cluster’s center, is the most massive single star known, with approximately 260 times the mass of our Sun. Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Webb ERO Production Team When new stars form, it’s the blue supergiants that shine brightest. The same region of space, just to the right of the central bright cluster of stars in Pismis 24, shows several stars against a black background in the Hubble image (at right), but many more stars and an eerie blue haze in the JWST image (at left).

Will AI make life less meaningful? A survey finds optimism hinges on whether humans keep control.

Big Think · 2026-11-07 17:32 UTC

OpenAI recently announced that its latest artificial intelligence model had solved, in a matter of weeks, more than 100 math problems that humans had worked on for years. The news sparked what seemed like an existential crisis among mathematicians, leaving some to wonder what role humans would have in the future of their field. It’s not just academics who are worried. In a new national survey, we found that Americans are more likely to see AI as a threat to meaning than as a resource that supports it. But that view depends on whether people think of AI as a tool that will remain under human control or as something that will become autonomous. Discussions about AI tend to focus on its practical costs and benefits, from job loss and cyberattacks to scientific and medical breakthroughs. Far less attention has been paid to its potential psychological effects, especially on our sense of meaning. Humans are a distinctly existential species.

Real Horrorshow!

MUBI Notebook · 2026-11-09 08:00 UTC

Main Stream Media Network (Jon Rafman, 2025). © Jon Rafman Courtesy the artist and Sprüth Magers. “The world isn’t a kind place, it’s wolves and devils,” says a character in Jon Rafman’s Main Stream Media Network: Proof of Concept (2025). With its hyperactive animation, haunting soundtrack, and twisted creepypasta tales of horror, the artist’s large-scale video work is more akin to a screaming conflagration than a feature film, a two-and-a-half hour transmission from hell. Modeled after the MTV of the early 1990s, a cultural moment Rafman views as the last example of a shared reality before the world cracked, the film is an attempt to capture that elusive thing: how it feels to be alive—and online—today. Over the last decade or so, Rafman has been exploring the various ways technology has shaped and shattered the contemporary mind, a project which has led him into increasingly fractured and unstable territory. (It has also, in recent years, earned him edgelord status, making him the darling of such fallen eminences as Kanye West and the futuristic fashion house Balenciaga.

MUBI Podcast: Encuentros | A Style of One’s Own

MUBI Notebook · 2026-11-05 13:23 UTC

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jk6unmAR9CI In this episode, cinematic tradition is explored as a refuge from artistic orphanhood. Valentina Maurel is a Costa Rican screenwriter and director. After completing her studies in Belgium, her graduation short film, Paul Is Here (2017), received First Prize at the Cannes Film Festival’s Cinéfondation, a program dedicated to supporting emerging filmmakers and showcasing student films. Her debut feature, I Have Electric Dreams (2022), was widely acclaimed by critics and recognized in the international competition at the Locarno Film Festival, where it won awards for Best Director, Best Actor and Best Actress. The film also received recognition at the San Sebastián, Ghent, Mar del Plata, Thessaloniki, India, and Guadalajara film festivals. With audacious honesty, Maurel has portrayed the struggles of young women grappling with untamed desire and caught in constant conflict with their parents, against the backdrop of San José’s turbulent urban life.

Filmmaker Survey | Lance Hammer

MUBI Notebook · 2026-11-05 08:00 UTC

Juliette Binoche and Tom Courtenay in Queen at Sea (Lance Hammer, 2026). With Queen at Sea (2026), American filmmaker Lance Hammer returns to direct his second film nearly two decades after his remarkable debut Ballast, which won the Grand Jury and directing awards at Sundance in 2008. Premiering in competition at the Berlin International Film Festival, the new film deservedly took home awards for Hammer’s direction and for actors Anna Calder-Marshall and Tom Courtenay, who play a long-married elderly couple. Leslie (Calder-Marshall), who suffers from dementia, is cared for at home by her husband Martin (Courtenay), who intentionally continues their sexual relationship even after it seems like his wife cannot consciously consent. When caught and confronted by Amanda (Juliette Binoche), Leslie’s daughter and Martin’s stepdaughter, he defends his actions as acts of love that offers his wife succor.

Can This Be Dixie?: Building the Hollywood South

MUBI Notebook · 2026-11-03 08:00 UTC

Hallelujah (King Vidor, 1929). The American South exists only in the imagination, yet it’s as real as sin. It cannot merely be the land situated beneath the Mason-Dixon (the historical survey line that traditionally demarcated Northern and Southern states), whose citizens fought under the banner of the Confederacy; one cannot ignore the obviously Southern states of West Virginia and Kentucky, or the political split between West and East Tennessee. It cannot be a shared culture or a shared history, for the residents of Jacksonville, Florida, find little in common with those families tucked deep in the Appalachian hollers or those ruling the oil-rich cities of eastern Texas. It is not a nation with shared laws, beliefs, or even religions. Instead, as the writers of the region have long known, the American South is a series of stories that overlap, contradict, and play off each other.

TIFF: The Market: The Review

MUBI Notebook · 2026-11-02 08:00 UTC

TIFF: The Market exhibition booth option. At the 51st Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF), which saw the inaugural edition of its official content market, the atmosphere was unmistakably different from its jubilee year. The spirit of nostalgic celebration and victory lapping from 2025's "TIFFty" celebration had evaporated, leaving behind the gritty residue of cinema as a commercial product. Lacking the elegance of “Marché du Film” at Cannes and the specificity of “European Film Market” at Berlinale, for their new industry initiative TIFF settled on a name that evokes the absurdity of local hero Matt Johnson’s Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie (2025). Its sans-serif, all-lowercase stylization will transport some Canadians to the grocery aisle, recalling Loblaws mogul Galen Weston’s “No Name” brand, a proudly generic grocery chain that prides itself on serving its customer base during tough economic times (while price-gouging them to death). “TIFF: The Market” attempted to do the same, stimulating the global screen sector amid layoffs and mergers through a $16.

Against the Grain: Music criticism can become critical again – here's how

The Wire Magazine · 2026-11-09 00:00 UTC

Popular music criticism can become relevant again by situating itself in broader theoretical frameworks, argues Rafael Lubner in The Wire 514 These are lean times for popular music criticism. Negotiating a gutted publishing landscape, amid a Spotify-led devaluation of listening, the form finds itself under serious threat. One index of criticism’s attenuated state is the narrowing frame of reference employed by critics to apprehend musical objects – rarely do we find new works in the visual arts, film or literature employed to understand transformations in music’s sound or form. Take, as a point of comparison, Greg Tate’s recently reissued Flyboy In The Buttermilk (reviewed in The Wire 513). Here are passionate defences of Miles Davis’s earth-shaking mid-1970s funk odysseys alongside surveys of Afrodiasporic art and reviews of writer Nathaniel Mackey and literary critic Henry Louis Gates Jr. Contemporary music criticism, by contrast, seems resolutely committed to understanding music as siloed from the non-musical.

Wire mix: Inside Prepared Piano

The Wire Magazine · 2026-10-27 00:00 UTC

To accompany her feature in The Wire 513, Jo Hutton compiles an annotated mix of tracks that make use of prepared piano The piano can be prepared by placing objects such as pins, screws, bolts, crocodile clips, ball bearings, kitchen utensils, magnets or tin foil on or between the strings. Its history dates back at least to the 1930s, when choreographer Syvilla Fort commissioned a dance piece from John Cage, who proposed his Bacchanale for percussion ensemble. But the performance theatre was too small to fit the intended ensemble, so Cage changed the sound of the house piano by adding screws and objects inside it to make it more percussive. This annotated mix includes tracks by some of the artists Jo Hutton speaks to as part of her feature in The Wire 513, plus pieces from across the history of the prepared piano.

The Wire Magazine · 2026-10-26 00:00 UTC

Listen to the music we played to Sarah Davachi during her Invisible Jukebox interview in The Wire 514 Each month in the magazine we play an artist or group a series of tracks which they are asked to comment on – with no prior knowledge of what they are about to hear. In The Wire 514 it is the turn of composer, organist and theorist Sarah Davachi. Here you can listen to a mix of the tracks that Emily Bick played to Davachi during the interview, which is published in full in The Wire 514. To find out what she said about them, subscribers can read the interview in our online magazine library here. Or you can buy a copy of the magazine in our online shop. But first, a brief biography of our subject: Canadian composer Sarah Davachi is known for her drone based works for organ, electronics, voice and chamber ensemble that explore extended durations, the psychoacoustics of space, and the subtleties of tuning, harmonic structures and emergent overtones.

Grande Nef de l'Île-des-Vannes Renovation / Chatillon Architectes

ArchDaily · 2026-11-09 11:00 UTC

Following seven years of closure, Chatillon Architectes implements contemporary solutions and state-of-the-art facilities, bringing this distinctive building back to life, first as an Olympic training site and then for its subsequent return to the local community. The first images of the restored Grande Nef de l'Île-des-Vannes sports complex in Paris have been revealed ahead of its role as an Olympic training facility. Featuring a sweeping parabolic roof and striking translucent side paneling, the unique structure was designed by Anatole Kopp, Lucien Metrich, and Pierre Chazanoff in 1971, and closed in 2018 due to decay and accessibility issues. Adapting the building for contemporary use, Chatillon Architectes has fully restored the structure, installing contemporary energy solutions, structural repairs, universal accessibility upgrades and state-of-the-art facilities, from acoustic paneling to sports flooring to lighting fixtures.

Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02639-6 Artificial intelligence (AI)-generated content increasingly saturates our information environment. Efforts to detect and remove it are failing. We propose that calling AI-generated content ‘slop’ is best understood as a social judgement: what a community recognizes as unwanted AI content. Studying AI slop this way makes it tractable, measurable and governable.

Light-pulse pairs reveal the femtosecond decay of an inner-shell hole in xenon atoms

Phys.org · 2026-11-10 02:20 UTC

Researchers at the UVSOR Synchrotron Facility (Institute for Molecular Science, Japan) and partner institutions have observed the decay of a xenon 4d core hole, an inner-shell vacancy, directly in the time domain. They used pairs of phase-coherent extreme ultraviolet pulses from a synchrotron to make the photoelectron wave packets they released interfere. The contrast of the interference fringes decreased over a few femtoseconds as the delay between the pulses increased. A model using literature core-hole lifetimes of about 6 femtoseconds reproduced this rapid decay of the fringe contrast. The study is published in the journal Physical Review A.

Evaluation of a therapeutic education program for patients with coronary heart disease in a Tunisian university hospital: A quasi-experimental study

PLOS ONE Biology · 2026-11-09 14:00 UTC

by Hela Ghali, Mohamed Ayoub Tlili, Aymen El Hraiech, Jihen Sahli, Sana Bhiri, Saoussen Layouni, Hend Ben Souda, Majdi Karray, Bruno Pavy, Asma Ben Cheikh, Chekib Zedini Background Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a major public health concern globally, including Tunisia. Therapeutic Patient Education (TPE) plays a crucial role in managing CVD and improving patient outcomes. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of a TPE program on the occurrence of major cardiovascular events in patients with coronary heart disease (CHD) in a Tunisian university hospital. Methods A quasi-experimental study was conducted over one year, involving 129 patients with CHD. The intervention group (n = 38) received a four-stage TPE program, while the control group (n = 91) received standard care. The control group met the same inclusion and non-inclusion criteria as the intervention group. It was constituted based on a 3:1 ratio. Patients in the intervention and control groups were recruited from the same department and during the same period to ensure comparability.

Effects of vitamin D supplementation on vitamin D status and physical performance in football players: A systematic review and meta-analysis

PLOS ONE Biology · 2026-11-06 14:00 UTC

by Jinfa Gu, Yu Zhang, Luhua Xiao Background/Objectives Low vitamin D status is frequently reported among athletes, but whether vitamin D supplementation improves physical performance in football players remains uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effects of vitamin D supplementation on serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] concentration, jump performance, sprint performance, aerobic capacity, and muscular performance in association football and futsal players. Methods PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from database inception to 31 May 2026. Controlled intervention studies comparing vitamin D supplementation with control conditions were eligible. Standardized mean differences were calculated as Hedges’ g and pooled using random-effects meta-analyses. Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed risk of bias using RoB 2 or ROBINS-I. The certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE. The protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261430873).

journal · primary · R4 · P4 · signal

Tranexamic acid for anemia in women of reproductive age: A systematic review of randomized trials

PLOS ONE Biology · 2026-11-06 14:00 UTC

by Sima Berendes, Katharine Ker, Hilary O. D. Critchley, Raoul Mansukhani, Ian Roberts Objective The global target to halve the prevalence of anemia by 2025 has not been met. New strategies are needed. This systematic review examined the effect of tranexamic acid on anemia, menstrual health and wellbeing in women of reproductive age. Methods We searched six databases from inception to 30 August 2025 and reference lists of seven related reviews. We included randomized trials comparing the effects of tranexamic acid with placebo or standard care on uterine bleeding. Eligible participants had normal menstrual bleeding or any type of non-pregnant abnormal uterine bleeding. Outcomes included hemoglobin concentration and anemia prevalence as the primary outcome, estimated blood loss, quality of life, thromboembolic events, and other adverse events. We conducted meta-analyses and assessed risk of bias (Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials) and the certainty of evidence. Results We included 17 trials in the review and 15 in the meta-analyses.

[Comment] Faster troponin, same time in the emergency department: what is next for acute coronary syndrome assessment?

The Lancet · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Emergency department overcrowding and access block are now among the most consequential patient-safety problems facing acute hospitals globally.1 The associated harm is measurable, dose-dependent, and has no clearly safe threshold beyond approximately 5 h.2 Patients presenting with possible myocardial infarction constitute a large and possibly modifiable share of the emergency department burden. Chest pain is the second most common reason for adult emergency department attendance in the USA, accounting for approximately 8 million encounters annually and around 5·5% of all emergency department visits.

The Lancet · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Across the available randomised trials, short-term adverse event rates were low with both pathways, but the pooled safety estimate remained imprecise. On average, earlier cardiac troponin retesting did not reduce emergency department length of stay or clearly increase direct discharge, and substantial between-study heterogeneity indicates that treatment effects might not translate uniformly across health-care systems. For hospitals considering transitioning from a 0/3 h to a 0/1 h pathway, implementation decisions should take broader diagnostic and organisational considerations into account.

Africa stands on the cusp of an El Niño-driven public health emergency, superimposed on an increasingly unpredictable and extreme climate. The Lancet · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

The treatment landscape of EGFR-mutated non-small-cell lung cancer harbouring exon 19 deletion or L858R mutations has advanced remarkably over the past two decades. Although acquired resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) is inevitable in most patients, novel compounds such as bispecific antibodies and antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs) have expanded the armamentarium of options after EGFR-TKI therapy. Following the global MARIPOSA-2 trial that showed superior progression-free survival (PFS) of amivantamab plus platinum–pemetrexed chemotherapy over platinum–pemetrexed chemotherapy alone in patients who have progressed on osimertinib,1 this is the second-line option preferred by major guidelines including the National Comprehensive Cancer Network and the European Society for Medical Oncology.

A Common Food Emulsifier Could Solve One of Rocketry’s Oldest Fuel Problems

Universe Today · 2026-11-09 17:22 UTC

In propulsion system design, engineers have long faced a trade-off between solid and liquid rocket fuels. Each has advantages and disadvantages, and in an effort to try to min/max the efficacy of different types of fuel, researchers have long placed an emphasis on a hybrid between solids and liquids - in other words they’ve been working with gels. Unfortunately, gels have their own sets of problems to deal with. But a new paper published by Pranay Mudaliar and Jerin John of Concordia in the journal Langmuir uses an uncommon ingredient to elegantly solve some of those problems, but which is typically used in a completely different area of human activity - lecithin.

A Stellar Odd Couple at an Unusual Stage of Evolution

Universe Today · 2026-11-09 14:39 UTC

Millisecond pulsars are fascinating objects that serve as natural clocks in the Universe. They form by drawing material and angular momentum from a companion. This mass transfer can rapidly accelerate the companion's evolution to a white dwarf. Astronomers have detected a millisecond pulsar's white dwarf companion that appears to be observed just as the mass transfer completed. They can still see some of the debris.

Phys.org Mollusks · 2026-10-20 13:30 UTC

Cephalopods, like the octopus, have specialized arms and suckers, but how these structures evolved from the simple bodies of their mollusk ancestors remains a mystery. Researchers from the University of Tokyo compared gene activity during embryonic development of cuttlefish, octopus and snail body parts. They found that several genes associated with appendage patterning showed expression along developing cephalopod arms, but no comparable patterns in developing suckers. Developing suckers instead expressed Ets1, a gene associated with early embryonic development in mollusks. The findings suggest cephalopods evolved suckers by reusing existing genes in new ways.

UK Mathematician Debunks Myth Around Parthenon's Optical Illusions

SoylentNews · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

hubie writes: Study challenges belief that temple's curves were designed to correct optical illusions that would have ruined its clean lines: A mathematician has uncovered what may be one of the longest-running myths in history after studying optical illusions and the Parthenon, the famed Greek temple that overlooks Athens. Scholars have marvelled at the building on the Acropolis hill for more than 2,000 years and heaped praise on its architects for their clever use of geometry. Its subtle curves are said to correct optical illusions that would have otherwise ruined the Parthenon's clean lines. But after a detailed investigation, and a flurry of mathematical modelling, Prof Alain Goriely at the University of Oxford has reached an awkward conclusion. The optical illusions the curves are meant to fix are either nonsense or practically imperceptible. In short, the illusions are themselves an illusion. In his study, Goriely traces the myth back to the 1st-century Roman architect and engineer Vitruvius who wrote about the Parthenon 400 years after its construction.

Immutable Leap To The Future

SoylentNews · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

quietus writes: In an immutable operating system the root file system is locked down (read-only) so that apps and users cannot change or break them. Instead of updating individual system files one by one, updates are installed as a single, complete package all at once, meaning that if anything ever goes wrong, the system can instantly roll back to the last safe, working version. These systems are mainly used with zero-touch installation installations (Internet-of-Things) or as container hosts; their rollback capabilities are appreciated when you're infected by malware, root kits and whatever exploitative flotsam-and-jetsam might hit you through the internet. The probably best known examples of immutable systems are Android and Chromebook, while an immutable Linux distro, bazzite, is making waves in the gaming world. In its latest release, Leap 16.1, SuSE Linux lets you choose between a conventional installation, or the installation of its immutable version of the same operating system.

Meet *Sshole, The Vulnerability That Lets Hackers SSH Into Linux Devices

SoylentNews · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

"Arthur T Knackerbracket" writes: https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/11/vulnerability-allows-attackers-to-log-into-some-linux-devices-sans-password/ Devices running some configurations of Alpine Linux, and possibly other distributions, are affected by a decade-old vulnerability that allows attackers to log into devices with no password. The vulnerability exists in the interaction between OpenSSH, the code library implementing SSH connections, and musl, a lightweight alternative to the libc library that, unlike most other Linux distributions, is used in Alpine. Further, OpenSSH using musl (pronounced muscle) must not use PAM (pluggable authentication modules), a framework that handles user authentication and account-access checks. Alpine is a lightweight, widely used Linux distribution. Other platforms may be affected if they use the same configurations. There are two other conditions necessary for successful exploitation. First, a system must have at least one user account that's accessible using a password that is hashed using the SHA256 or SHA512 functions.

Hide your slop PR descriptions behind <details><summary>

Simon Willison's Weblog · 2026-11-09 04:25 UTC

Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work - I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today's coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions. They're too good at describing the work The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That's a lot of information to absorb. It's not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop! It's very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as "I'm not reading all of that". It doesn't matter how accurate or useful the information is, I'm instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me! I want human editorial judgement.

Research: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust I was out walking the dog when I got curious about how easy/difficult it would be to write a SQLite C extension that adds a parse_number() function for turning strings like -$1,234.56 or '12.5%' into numeric values that could be summed and sorted. datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages

Simon Willison's Weblog · 2026-11-07 23:57 UTC

datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages I was looking at the Firefox network panel today when I noticed that requests to a Datasette table page were triggering an HTTP prefetch to the next page of rows in that table. This was happening because Datasette pages serve an HTTP link header like this: link: ; rel="next" This is bad. A tiny fraction of the visitors to one of those pages will click the "next" link, which means for everyone else their browser is fetching unnecessary data and the Datasette server is having to render an entire page that then gets thrown away. I dug in and learned that Firefox has an issue that has been open for 24 years about this behavior... And one of the early comments on that issue links to my blog post from 2002 complaining about this feature. I hadn't just forgotten that I had written about it, I had forgotten the feature entirely! LWN.net · 2026-11-07 09:49 UTC

The Asahi Linux developers have put out a new report on their progress toward a Linux distribution for Apple devices. Some time ago, we were made aware of multiple attempts to exploit our permissive licensing to hijack our work, with a direct view to replacing the project and aggressively monetising Linux on Apple Silicon. In some extreme cases, in-development feature code was being lifted straight out of our personal forks and published without attribution or lazily rewritten with LLM assistance to obfuscate its origin. The MIT licence explicitly allows this, and has no carveouts to protect against bad faith actors. As such, we made the difficult decision to begin the process of transitioning all of our repositories to the GNU General Public License version 2 or later. Going forward all Asahi Linux code will be licenced under strong copyleft licences only. Those who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it.

Specifically, let's highlight seven major essential security properties of AOS here: No Shell + No SSH + No Language Interpreters. By default AOS does not install a UNIX shell, nor makes remote access via SSH available on the nodes. Moreover, we do not install any of the usual language interpreters (Python, Perl, …) by default. For most nodes a shell or interpreted language support is not required and it removes a whole class of attacks. Signed Images Only. Bliki: LLM Voice

Martin Fowler · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Sometimes when I read a post, I get the growing feeling that I'm reading the output of an LLM. I can't necessarily define why, although there are the common tells (it's not the em-dashes, it's the load-bearing tapestries). As I do this my desire to read on atrophies, sometimes to the point of revulsion There are tools out there that claim to be able to tell the difference between LLM-written prose and the old-fashioned biological product. I'm wary of them, partly due skeptism about their accuracy, but also because it rather misses the point. The reaction to LLM-Voice is a human one, that sense that we are in an uncanny valley of prose. By the time I'd reach for a tool to tell me what I'm reading, it's already too late, even if it confidently tells me there's no LLM present. I'm also suspicious of my own ability to accurately recognize LLM voice. Language changes over time, so a common sign of age is complaining about the language of the youngs. I'm inclined to bristle at prose that talks about “adopting a new sales motion,” or “a sharp round-up of news”.

Why are good developers so wary of agentic development?

Martin Fowler · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

TL;DR Good developers’ caution about agentic development comes from knowing that built isn’t the same as working in production. I’ve been surprised by how many excellent developers have been hesitant to go all in on coding agents. These are people who usually try new ways of working before anyone else and in many cases invent new tools and practices that support building the application well. So why have we had so much reluctance? The easy (lazy?) answer is that they love writing code, or they’re worried about their jobs. I’m sure that’s true for some people, some of the time. And I know it is true for some of the developers I talk to but I always felt there was something else, another fear hiding behind those obvious ones. When we put together the Technology Radar every six months I try to block out a chunk of time for us to do an open space. In September, a discussion we had on agentic development, which pushed it to its limits, finally helped me see clearly what that fear is. Building it right Thoughtworkers care deeply about building the right thing and building it right.

Introducing TPU Sync: Fast KV cache and weight transfer for inference and RL on TPU

Google Cloud Blog · 2026-11-09 13:00 UTC

As frontier AI evolves from stateless single-turn prompts to million-token agents, disaggregated serving, and continuous reinforcement learning (RL), the primary bottleneck in AI infrastructure has shifted from raw compute to orchestrating live model state — both the contextual state held in massive key-value (KV) caches during inference and the parameter state updated and broadcast from trainers to rollout samplers during RL. Whenever this state is trapped inside a single chip's memory or stalled on network transfers, AI accelerators sit idle. We designed TPU Sync from first principles to serve as the model-state layer across TPU clusters — built on the architectural insight that accelerator High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), host DRAM, shared storage, and the data center network (DCN) should operate as a single, co-designed memory hierarchy. An open-source, native C++ library, TPU Sync moves TPU-tiled tensors directly across this hierarchy with asynchronous DMA transfers that overlap data movement with active computation.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Now generally available: GKE dynamic slicing for higher resilience, and efficiency for TPUs

Google Cloud Blog · 2026-11-09 13:00 UTC

Running large-scale AI workloads on TPU and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) requires infrastructure that adapts as fast as your models change. Dynamic Slicing is generally available on GKE, which decouples logical TPU slice formation from physical nodepool provisioning. Compared to creating a static nodepool for each TPU slice, dynamic slicing reduces AI workload startup times by up to 5x and workload recovery by 4.5x — maximizing TPU goodput, efficiency, and workload resilience at scale. Beyond one workload, one nodepool Previously, managing TPU capacity at GKE standard required separate, fixed TPU slice topology nodepools, increasing startup times and complexity while preventing multi-host nodepools from hosting multiple AI workloads. Changing workload needs meant manually deleting and recreating nodepools. Additionally, this tight coupling created large failure domains where a single hardware fault crashed an entire slice, slowing recovery while reprovisioning.

Announcing the Workload Conformance Working Group

We are excited to announce that the Kubernetes community now has a Workload Conformance Working Group. The working group is writing a shared standard for how workloads behave at runtime on Kubernetes. To get it right, we need input from the people who build those workloads and from the people who run the clusters they're deployed on. Why workloads need a shared standard Certified Kubernetes tests the cluster, and Kubernetes AI Conformance tests whether a cluster can run AI and ML workloads. Nothing comparable exists for the workloads themselves, so cluster operators still check each application by hand before routine maintenance or a Kubernetes upgrade. The problems they find are familiar. A routine node drain is often how you discover that an application can't tolerate disruption. An upgrade can break an application that still depends on a removed API version. Others show up in day-to-day operation: workloads that ask for privileges they don't need, or reserve resources they never use. Kubernetes already documents much of this, including security and handling disruptions.

Making Failure Diagnosis Reliable with Pensive AI

By Praneeth Yenugutala, Victor Dusa, Anastasia Samoilova, Megan Ren, Justin Wei, Marcelo Mayworm At Netflix, data and machine learning practitioners run millions of workloads each day across orchestration systems and compute engines such as Titus, Spark, Trino, and Druid. On peak days, roughly 100,000 workloads fail. When workloads fail, the failure itself is only the beginning. Someone still needs to find the useful signal in several logs, decide whether the cause sits in their code or the platform, and determine whether to retry, reconfigure, or escalate. Even a small share of difficult failures can consume engineering time, waste compute, and interrupt critical data pipelines. Our first answer to that problem was Pensive, an auto-diagnosis and remediation system in Netflix’s data platform. Pensive collected logs from failed workloads, used regular expressions and hand-authored Java rules to extract and classify errors, then passed retry or remediation guidance to products such as Maestro. It made ~ 50% of failures self-service and, in some cases, automatic.

The Shift to cgroup v2 in Kubernetes: What You Need to Know

Kubernetes Blog · 2026-10-06 18:00 UTC

In Linux, cgroups (control groups) are a kernel feature used for managing system resources. Kubernetes uses cgroups to allocate resources like CPU and memory to containers, ensuring that applications run smoothly without interfering with each other. With the release of Kubernetes v1.31, support for v1 cgroup management moved into maintenance mode. Support for v2 cgroup management has been stable since Kubernetes v1.25. Compared with cgroup v1, cgroup v2 provides a single unified hierarchy, a more consistent interface, and a stronger foundation for resource isolation and modern resource-management features. Deprecation of cgroup v1 Kubernetes has deprecated cgroup v1. Starting with Kubernetes v1.35, failCgroupV1 defaults to true, so the kubelet does not start on a cgroup v1 node by default. Administrators can temporarily set failCgroupV1: false in the kubelet configuration file, but removal will follow the Kubernetes deprecation policy. Further removal work is tracked in KEP-5573: Remove cgroup v1 support. If you are still on a release older than v1.

Scaling Kubernetes Workloads with Node Swap

Kubernetes Blog · 2026-10-05 18:00 UTC

Memory is often the first hard limit a Kubernetes cluster hits. Nodes run out of RAM long before they run out of CPU, and the new wave of agentic AI workloads makes this worse. These workloads demand large memory footprints to start up and run untrusted code, then sit idle waiting for the next prompt. That idle but resident memory is expensive, and it caps how many pods a node can hold. This is where swap helps. Kubernetes support for running nodes with swap enabled reached General Availability in v1.34, and by backing that swap with fast NVMe solid state drives (SSDs), a node can page out dormant memory and pack in far more pods. This post explains how we benchmarked that approach across three workloads, including CI/CD kernel builds, sandboxed headless browsers, and isolated Python runtimes; we found density gains of up to 3×, often with little or no latency cost.

Can Agentic Robotics Solve Robotics’ Data Scaling Problem?

IEEE Spectrum Robotics · 2026-11-09 14:00 UTC

Robotics companies are investing heavily in the belief that data will solve the most difficult problems in robotics. Once AI systems have ingested enough data from human demonstrations, the thinking goes, robots will be able to perform the vast majority of the manual tasks that humans now do. There are even robotics companies that exist solely to collect training data and sell it to other robotics companies in pursuit of this goal. But whether data will finally bring us general-purpose robots is an open question. Nobody knows how much data would be necessary, what kind of data is important, or whether something else might be missing. And there are other problems with a reliance on massive amounts of data: the resulting AI algorithms are essentially black boxes, which despite their high performance are difficult or impossible for humans to understand. This characteristic is becoming increasingly concerning in commercial deployments, where robots must be flexible, reliable, and safe.

Last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun. Phobos, the Martian moon named for the Greek god of fear and panic, was transiting the solar disk. Too small to darken the pale, dust-tinged sky, but orbiting close enough to eclipse a significant fraction of the Sun, Phobos passed in less than a minute. NASA’s Perseverance rover captured Phobos passing in front of the Sun from the surface of Mars.ASU/MSSS/SSI/JPL-Caltech/NASA The tiny moon, with its murky origins, is an enigma, and one whose makeup and history could tell us much about Mars and the wider solar system. And now the international Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, which successfully launched on 20 October, seeks to explore that mystery with an unprecedented series of landings on the unknown surface of Phobos. This mission brings unusual challenges—for example, designing an orbit to study a microgravity moon orbiting a much larger planet.

Autonomous Airships Keep Tabs on Energy Infrastructure

IEEE Spectrum Aerospace · 2026-10-29 14:00 UTC

Inspecting thousands of kilometers of power lines, pipelines, or rail tracks is an expensive and time-consuming business. It’s typically done by helicopters, which are costly, noisy, and polluting. French startup HyLight thinks uncrewed airships could be a cheaper, more environmentally friendly alternative. The company has developed a 12-meter-long blimp powered by a hydrogen fuel cell capable of staying airborne for up to 10 hours and traveling 350 kilometers per day. The airship carries an array of sensors for inspection, including high-precision cameras, lidar, and methane detectors. HyLight uses AI models (some developed in-house, some off the shelf) to automatically analyze collected data and identify more than 50 types of maintenance issues. The French civil aviation authority and the European Union Aviation Safety Agency have both granted permission for HyLight’s airships—which have so far logged more than 750 flight hours—to operate beyond visual line of sight.

How Beta Technologies Is Clearing the Runway for Electric Flight

IEEE Spectrum Aerospace · 2026-10-28 13:00 UTC

In the cockpit of Beta Technologies’ Alia CX300, pilot Chris Caputo steers onto Runway 33 at Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport in Vermont. Cleared for takeoff, he releases the brakes and nudges the throttle forward. At the back of the aircraft, the five-blade pusher propeller snaps awake, and the Alia bolts forward. There’s no shriek of a turbofan spooling up, no shudder of a piston engine, and no wait for thrust. Just the low hum of an electric motor and a shove of instant acceleration. Within a few seconds, we’re at 85 knots (almost 160 kilometers per hour), and Caputo rotates the nose upward. The runway drops abruptly away as we climb. Gaining speed and altitude, we head northwest over Lake Champlain. Through the wraparound canopy, I watch the hunched shoulders of Vermont’s Green Mountains shrink under the right wing, with New York’s taller Adirondacks to the left. Caputo, a former Air Force fighter pilot, flicks the control stick hard left, then right.

The skies are becoming dangerously crowded—not with planes but with interference and jamming disrupting many of the 30,000 radio frequencies that civil aviation relies upon. Your Robot’s Safety Functions Already Work. What If the Input Lies?

IEEE Spectrum Robotics · 2026-10-27 16:14 UTC

This article is brought to you by VicOne. A mobile robot slows for someone in a hallway. A collaborative arm eases its movement as a worker approaches. A humanoid pauses to let a person pass. Each response depends on information about the robot or its surroundings: a distance reading, a position estimate, or a stop signal. But what happens when one of those inputs is wrong, and the robot still responds exactly as designed? The mobile robot reads the hallway as clear while someone is still there. The arm estimates that the worker is farther away. The humanoid does not receive a stop signal as a person crosses its path. In each case, a fault could cause that mismatch. So could deliberate manipulation. At VicOne LAB R7, we examine how manipulated inputs can change robot behavior — and what that means for the systems meant to keep people safe. How an untrusted input can change a robot’s behavior A robot does more than measure its surroundings. It may interpret what it sees and hears to decide what to do next. Information placed in its environment can therefore influence its actions.

Will Fiber-Optic Cables Finally Get Made in Orbit?

IEEE Spectrum Aerospace · 2026-10-26 12:00 UTC

In a lab in Luxembourg in 2024, engineers at Flawless Photonics unpacked a spool of glass fiber that had just returned from the International Space Station (ISS). As they threaded it onto their rewinding machine, the machine jammed—as happens sometimes—and they braced for the usual outcome: The fiber would snap. This time, though, nothing broke. It was an early hint that their experiment might have been successful. The Flawless Photonics team had set out to draw fibers of a heavy-metal fluoride glass called ZBLAN—named for its other components of zirconium, barium, lanthanum, aluminum, and sodium (chemical symbol Na)—in microgravity, aiming to achieve superior optical and physical properties. “We realized, wow, that fiber is much stronger than the stuff we had produced on Earth,” says Hubert Moser, the company’s cofounder and CTO. ZBLAN Fiber’s Microgravity Advantages Photonics engineers have been intrigued by ZBLAN for decades because it can, in theory, transmit light with 1 percent of the loss of silica.

AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security

IEEE Spectrum · 2026-11-09 16:25 UTC

This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast. Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance. However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof?

How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?

IEEE Spectrum Aerospace / IEEE Spectrum · 2026-11-06 15:00 UTC

Last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun. Phobos, the Martian moon named for the Greek god of fear and panic, was transiting the solar disk. Too small to darken the pale, dust-tinged sky, but orbiting close enough to eclipse a significant fraction of the Sun, Phobos passed in less than a minute. NASA’s Perseverance rover captured Phobos passing in front of the Sun from the surface of Mars.ASU/MSSS/SSI/JPL-Caltech/NASA The tiny moon, with its murky origins, is an enigma, and one whose makeup and history could tell us much about Mars and the wider solar system. And now the international Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, which successfully launched on 20 October, seeks to explore that mystery with an unprecedented series of landings on the unknown surface of Phobos. This mission brings unusual challenges—for example, designing an orbit to study a microgravity moon orbiting a much larger planet.

Eventually a manager would tap me on the shoulder and hand me a promotion (probably with a nice little speech). That plan stalled my career for about five years. I switched jobs twice, kept my head down, read a stack of programming books, and sometimes pulled 12-hour days. I was never promoted. At my third job, out of frustration, I started interviewing at other companies and almost immediately got an offer for a senior engineer role. So I went back to my job and quit. My team was blindsided. I liked my manager and the people I worked with, and they came back with a counteroffer. Then someone from HR asked me, “Why didn’t you just ask us?” Honestly, it never occurred to me.
